title: Opinions & Ideas
description: Words for saying what you think, weighing things up and disagreeing gently: menurut saya, setuju, mungkin, memang, justru and the rest.

items.registerNotes: Bagaimana pendapat Anda? is the polite way to ask what someone thinks; with friends, Gimana menurut kamu?
items.pitfallNote: Don't confuse it with pendapatan, which means income.

items.registerNotes: Menurut saya, … is the everyday way to say I think or in my opinion. It also cites a source: menurut dokter (according to the doctor).
items.pitfallNote: Saya berpikir bahwa … is a word-for-word I think that and sounds stiff; start with menurut saya instead.

items.registerNotes: Saya pikir … works for I think, though menurut saya sounds more natural for opinions. Saya pikir-pikir dulu, ya (I'll think about it) politely turns down a sale or an offer.
items.pitfallNote: Saya kira … means I thought, usually about something that turned out wrong: Saya kira tokonya sudah tutup (I thought the shop had closed).

items.registerNotes: Saya setuju (I agree), or setuju dengan Anda for agreeing with someone. Setuju on its own is a quick yes to a suggestion.
items.cultureNote: Flat disagreement can feel rude. People soften it: Saya kurang setuju (I don't quite agree), or Iya, tapi … (Yes, but …).

items.registerNotes: Apa alasannya? asks for the reason. Said with a certain tone it means an excuse: Itu cuma alasan (That's just an excuse).
Tidak masalah (No problem) answers thanks or an apology; casually, Nggak masalah. Masalahnya, … introduces the catch: Masalahnya, saya tidak punya waktu (The thing is, I don't have time).
Common in speech and at work: Solusinya apa? (What's the solution?) Jalan keluar, literally a way out, is the everyday alternative.
Ide bagus (Good idea) is a common reply to a suggestion.
items.pitfallNote: For I have no idea, say Saya tidak tahu (or Nggak tahu); Saya tidak punya ide means you have no ideas to offer.

items.registerNotes: Kenyataannya, … means in reality or the fact is, often before something disappointing. Nyata on its own means real.
Mungkin besok (Maybe tomorrow). Tidak mungkin means that's impossible, or no way.
items.cultureNote: A polite no often comes as mungkin or Lihat nanti, ya (We'll see). If an invitation gets a mungkin, don't count on a yes.

items.registerNotes: On its own, pasti is a confident of course, and belum pasti means it isn't certain yet. Before a description it makes a sure guess: Pasti capek, ya? (You must be tired.)
Sepertinya mau hujan (Looks like it's going to rain). It also softens an opinion: Sepertinya kurang cocok (I don't think it quite works); in casual speech, kayaknya.
Softens something unwelcome: Sebenarnya saya kurang suka pedas (Actually, I don't really like spicy food). Casual speech says sebenernya.
A little formal: Tentu saja boleh (Of course you may). In everyday speech people often say Tentu, Pasti, or Iya, dong with friends.
Agrees with or admits something: Memang enak, tapi mahal (True, it's good, but it's expensive). Casual speech says emang, and Memang begitu means that's just how it is.

items.english: on the contrary; precisely, in fact
items.registerNotes: Turns an expectation around: Hujan? Justru enak untuk tidur (Rain? That's actually perfect for sleeping). Justru itu means that's exactly the point.
items.pitfallNote: Justru and malah overlap; justru tends to put forward the real point, while malah usually reports an unwelcome surprise.

items.registerNotes: For something that goes the opposite way from what was expected, often with a sigh: Saya sudah minum obat, tapi malah tambah pusing (I took medicine, but I feel even dizzier).

items.english: for example, for instance; say, suppose
items.registerNotes: Misalnya? on its own asks for an example. It also floats a suggestion: Bagaimana kalau, misalnya, jam tujuh? (How about, say, seven?)
Contohnya? asks for an example. It also means a sample, and memberi contoh is to give, or set, an example.
Sounds formal in conversation, where people say Apa bedanya? (What's the difference?) Beda also means different: Rasanya beda (It tastes different).
In conversation people more often use sama (the same): Rasanya sama (They taste the same). In maths, persamaan is an equation.
Itu keputusan Anda (It's your decision). The usual phrase is mengambil keputusan, literally to take a decision.
Tidak ada pilihan lain (There's no other choice). Pilih is to choose: Silakan pilih (Please choose).
Kalau ada kesempatan, … (If I get the chance, …). Terima kasih atas kesempatannya is a polite thank-you at the end of a talk or an interview.
items.pitfallNote: It's chance as in opportunity; chance as in likelihood is kemungkinan.

items.registerNotes: Both a single experience and experience built up over time: pengalaman pertama (a first experience), pengalaman kerja (work experience). The verb is mengalami, to go through.
Tergantung on its own is a complete answer. Put what it depends on straight after: Tergantung cuaca (It depends on the weather); tergantung pada is more formal.
